logline: A royal physician stripped of his position after a court conspiracy retreats to a remote village and discovers his true calling - healing not just bodies but the emotional wounds of Joseon-era patients.

renewal.note: Two-season run concluded February 9, 2023. Adapted from a 2016 Korea Story Contest Excellence Award-winning novel by Lee Eun-so. No further seasons announced.

bollymeter.basis: Kim Min-jae's warm central performance and the show's unusually gentle approach to historical drama earned loyal viewers; Season 1 averaged 1,090,000 viewers (Nielsen). Critics and audiences praised the healing-drama tone while noting pacing issues in the middle stretch.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 of Poong, the Joseon Psychiatrist moves at the pace of its protagonist's own healing: deliberately, with occasional detours. Kim Min-jae's Yoo Se-poong is a disgraced royal physician who finds purpose in a village clinic, and the show is at its best when it treats the emotional ailments of its supporting characters with as much seriousness as the physical ones. The historical medical framing is distinctive - psychiatry as Joseon-era practice is an original premise with genuine dramatic potential. Critics clustered on the warmth of the ensemble and the chemistry between Kim Min-jae and Kim Hyang-gi, while flagging that the plot's conspiracy threads are less compelling than the village episodics. Season 1 averaged 1.09 million viewers according to Nielsen Korea, a solid baseline for cable drama in a competitive slot.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere sets up the fall-from-grace origin with efficiency and lands the central character in the village that will become his redemption arc. The tonal register - warm rather than tragic - is established from the first episode.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Yoo Se-poong's first encounter at the village clinic signals that this is a drama more interested in emotional healing than court intrigue.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 averaged 576,000 viewers against Season 1's 1.09 million (Nielsen Korea), a significant drop that reflected audience consensus: the second run struggled to find new dramatic territory within the same village setting.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 returned to the same clinic and largely the same character dynamics, and the viewership halving from Season 1 to Season 2 - from 1.09 million down to 576,000 (Nielsen Korea) - tells the story more cleanly than any critical summary. The ensemble remains likeable and Kim Min-jae's commitment never wavers, but the writers do not open up the narrative in ways that justify a second season. The emotional healing episodics that distinguished Season 1 feel familiar here, and the court intrigue threads that were the weakest part of Season 1 carry more weight without becoming more interesting. For those who invested in the characters, Season 2 provides closure; as standalone drama it is considerably thinner.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 contracts the ambition of Season 1 - same village, similar cases, with viewership nearly halving to 576,000 (Nielsen Korea) in material that works best as a one-season character study.
